abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: This work aims to analyse the toxicity of propyl-propane thiosulfinate (PTS) and propyl-propane thiosulfonate (PTSO), two organosulfur compounds, in long-lived winter (also known as diutinus bees) and short-lived spring honey bees. Acute toxicity assays were performed by contact and oral exposure, using the insecticide dimethoate as toxic standard. These compounds are derived from Allium cepa and have previously reported antimicrobial and weak insecticidal activity, and their potential use in crop protection requires a honeybee risk assessment under the new EFSA pollinator protection guidelines. Additionally, the concentrations at which honey bees do not voluntarily ingest each compound were assessed through an antifeedant activity test. In both cohorts, the LD50 of PTS and PTSO are higher than the hypothetical application dose (1 µg/bee). Long-lived winter honey bees were found to be more resistant to both compounds than short-lived spring honey bees. Assessment of the effects of exposure to both compounds combined showed no synergism. Neither cohort voluntarily ingested PTS or PTSO at 10 µg/µl. While partial ingestion was observed at 2 and 4 µg/µl, at 1 µg/µl or lower voluntary ingestion occurred at levels comparable to the control, without any observed mortality. These findings indicate that, at field relevant doses, PTS and PTSO are compatible with honey bee safety under acute exposure and warrant further field and chronic-exposure evaluation.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Pollinators are directly related to the reproduction of plant species and the conservation of ecosystems1. Pollination, identified by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) as a relevant ecosystem service2, takes part in the preservation of wild plant biodiversity3 and enhances the quality and yield of global cros production4,5. The western honey bee (Apis mellifera Linnaeus; Hymenoptera: Apidae) is, among a diverse group of vertebrates and invertebrates, the most important pollinator from both an ecological and economic point of view6. Honey bees play a key role in agricultural ecosystems since, as estimated by FAO, they are primarily responsible for the pollination of 71 of the 100 species that provide 90% of food worldwide7,8. There is evidence of a significant decline in bees and other insect pollinatos populations9–11, which leads to the disappearance of species that rely on them directly or indirectly and threatens food security 12. The main factors contributing to this decline include infestation by Varroa destructor, which has developed increasing tolerance to commonly used acaricides13, beekeeping management practices14,15, agricultural practices and the use of pesticides, climate change, loss of natural habitat heterogeneity and transformation of the landscape16–18.

The European Commission presented in 2018 the EU Pollinators Initiative, the first coordinated EU framework aimed at improving pollinator protection and reducing harmful non-target effects of pesticides. This initiative emphasizes the need to reduce the use of more hazardous synthetic pesticides and adopt more sustainable pest-management strategies19. In parallel, the EU Farm to Fork Strategy sets a target of reducing the use of chemical pesticides by 50% by 2030 and promoting integrated pest-management approaches20.

In this context, organosulfur compounds propyl-propane thiosulfinate (PTS) and propyl-propane thiosulfonate (PTSO) derived from onion (Allium cepa) have garnered increasing attention due to their functional properties, including flavouring, antimicrobial, antiparasitic, antitumoral, and immunomodulatory activities, among others21–26. Both are volatile compounds that are formed through dismutation or disproportionation reactions from propiin27, which is a natural constituent of fresh onion bulb tissue28.

This has led to an expansion of their potential applications within the agri-food sector, where their diverse properties could make them valuable as active agents for pest management or as promising ingredients for both human and animal nutrition29,30. The study of the possible applications of these organosulfur compounds in agriculture has recently started. Previous research on the inhibitory effect of PTS and PTSO on growth and mycotoxin production of Fusarium species in vitro and in situ on artificially inoculated wheat, oats and maize demonstrated that these compounds significantly reduced both parameters in vitro. Efficacy in situ depended on the specific Fusarium species-toxin pathosystem and water availability31. PTS and PTSO have also been shown to have in vitro and in vivo antifungal activity against Verticillium dahliae, the causal agent of Verticillium wilt, which is considered the most devastating soilborne fungal disease affecting olive trees (Olea europaea L. var. europaea). Specifically, in planta trials demonstrated that these compounds reduce disease-related parameters and contribute to the control of the phytopathogen at 0.5 µg/µl32. Additionally, another study assessed the effects of an onion extract formulation rich in organosulfur compounds, including PTS and PTSO, on olive trees under various conditions, including abiotic stress and Verticillium wilt33. These in planta trials demonstrated that the concentrations tested are not toxic to olive trees. A recent study has demonstrated the antimicrobial activity of PTS and PTSO against a wide range of phytopathogenic bacteria and fungi in vitro, and also has shown their repellent and biocidal properties against the cotton aphid, Aphis gossypii Glover (Hemiptera: Aphididae)34. Aphis gossypii is a major agricultural pest that acts as a vector for many serious plant viruses, such as the cucumber mosaic virus35. These results suggest that the properties of both organosulfur compounds are of great interest for the agricultural sector, which has recently experienced an increase in the demand for new environmentally-friendly non-synthetic PPPs36.

With the aim of further exploring the agri-food applications of these compounds, numerous toxicity assays, both in cell lines and in studies on murine models of chronic and acute toxicity, have been conducted, demonstrating their safe use37–41. The Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) has developed toxicity testing guidelines for PPPs on Apis species42, which have been validated by EFSA according to regulation (EU) 1107/2009 and accepted internationally43. As a result of the standardization of toxicity evaluation methods, extensive empirical data regarding the potential impact of chemical compounds that can be found in products available on the market have been obtained and compiled in the literature as well as in databases44,45. While a limited number of studies assessing the toxicity of garlic extracts in honey bees have been found46,47, no data was found in the literature regarding the toxic potential of PTS and PTSO on pollinating organisms.

Taking these facts into account, the aim of the present study was to investigate for the first time the in vivo toxicity of PTS and PTSO in the western honey bee. To achieve this, contact and oral toxicity assays were conducted on short-lived spring and long-lived overwinter honey bees (diutinus bees), explicitly comparing their susceptibility to assess the influence of cohort-specific physiological traits. The inclusion of diutinus bees was motivated by climate change leading to increasingly warmer winters, especially in Mediterranean regions, which result in greater overwinter activity48,49. Combined exposure to PTS and PTSO was also evaluated to determine whether any synergistic effects occurred. Additionally, the voluntary intake of PTS and PTSO was assessed using an antifeedant activity test. Overall, the study was conceived as an exploratory, acute toxicity assessment conducted in accordance with OECD Test Guidelines, which are internationally accepted reference methods for honey bee acute toxicity testing, including by EFSA.

sec.title: Acute toxicity
sec.p: The contact toxicity of the organosulfur compounds PTS and PTSO on long-lived winter and short-lived spring honey bees was evaluated through a limit test. Results are shown in Figures 1 and 2. The mortality in the control groups, whicht included solvents (acetone and polysorbate) and water, was 0% in winter and spring trials. Moreover, the mortality of the toxic standard (dimethoate) was 100% in both cases. Regarding the tested products, no mortality was observed in either winter or spring honey bees when applying 1 µg/bee of PTS or PTSO, which represents the hypothetical application concentration for field conditions. Long-lived winter honey bees were found to be resistant to PTS and PTSO at higher concentrations when applied topically. No significant differences were observed between the mortality percentage of winter honey bees treated with 100 µg of PTS or PTSO (6.67% and 4.44%, respectively) compared to the control (p > 0.05). The average mortality of this cohort when treated with 50 µg of each compound (i.e., with 100 µg of active ingredients) was only 4.44%. This was indicative of the absence of synergy between both Allium compounds. Contact with 200 µg a.i./bee (100 µg of PTS and 100 µg of PTSO) doubled the mortality rate of the group treated with 50 µg/bee of each compound, indicating the dose dependency of the contact toxicity of PTS and PTSO. On the other hand, PTS and PTSO significantly affected short-lived spring honey bees’ survival when applied topically at 100 µg/bee (p < 0.05), reaching 100% and 95.55% mortality after 24 h of exposure respectively. Although this dosage represents a 100-fold increase over the proposed application dose under field conditions, given their potential contact toxicity in spring honey bees, a test was conducted to determine the LD50. After 24 h, the LD50 values for PTS and PTSO were 31.24 and 35.15 µg/bee, respectively. These values, presented in Table 1, are above the hypothetical application dose (1000 µg/ml). As expected from the biological properties, the mortality rate did not increase after 48 h of exposure in any contact toxicity test performed. Furthermore, sublethal damage was not observed in living individuals at the different study times or concentrations tested.

caption.p: Determination of acute contact toxicity in long-lived winter honey bees by Limit Test. Mortality results are expressed as percentage. Bars with different letters indicate significant differences according to Tukey test (p < 0.05).

Determination of acute contact toxicity in short-lived spring honey bees by Limit Test. Mortality results are expressed as percentage. Bars with different letters indicate significant differences according to Tukey test (p < 0.05).
LD50 contact and oral of PTS and PTSO for short-lived spring honeybees, expressed in µg of test substance per bee, and 95% confidence intervals (CI) for each experimental group.

sec.p: Figures 3 and 4 summarise the effects of exposure to oral doses of PTS and PTSO separately and combined. The average mortality for water, acetone and polysorbate controls did not exceed 10% at the end of the test, whereas oral administration of dimethoate caused 100% honey bee mortality after 24 h of exposure. These results meet the criteria in the OECD guideline for the validity of the results. Neither PTS nor PTSO resulted in any toxic effect in either cohort when tested at 1 µg/bee. Furthermore, no increase in toxicity was observed when the combinations of 0.5 µg PTS and 0.5 µg PTSO, and 1 µg PTS and 1 µg PTSO were ingested. As in the acute contact toxicity test, differences were observed in the tolerance of long-lived winter and short-lived spring honey bees to oral exposure to combined PTS and PTSO at 100 µg/bee (100 times the normal usage dose of the individual compounds). No significant differences were observed in the 100 µg/bee PTS, 100 µg/bee PTSO and 50 µg PTS + 50 µg PTSO treatment groups compared to control groups (p > 0.05). The oral exposure to 100 µg PTS + 100 µg PTSO caused 8.89% mortality (p < 0.05) in long-lived winter bees due to the doubling of the total amount of compounds administered. In contrast, no short-lived spring honey bees survived after ingestion of 100 µg PTS, PTSO or their two combinations (50 µg PTS + 50 µg PTSO, and 100 µg PTS + 100 µg PTSO). According to the OECD guideline for acute oral toxicity test, a study for the determination of LD50 values of PTS and PTSO was conducted. After 24 h, the LD50 values, shown in Table 1, were 19.96 for PTS and 22.25 for PTSO. As with the LD50 contact test, the hypothetical application dose (1000 µg/ml) is well below the oral LD50. Mortality rate after the ingestion of 20 µg of PTS was 53.33%, and in all living honey bees sublethal effects were observed. In the case of PTSO, sublethal effects were observed in the study group exposed to 25 µg, in which a mortality rate of 66.67% was recorded. In both cases, sublethal damages observed were difficulty flying and atypical muscle movements. Results did not change after 48 h in any oral toxicity test performed.

caption.p: Determination of acute oral toxicity in long-lived winter honey bees by Limit Test. Mortality results are expressed as percentage. Bars with different letters indicate significant differences according to Tukey test (p < 0.05).

Determination of acute oral toxicity in short-lived spring honey bees by Limit Test. Mortality results are expressed as percentage. Bars with different letters indicate significant differences according to Tukey test (p < 0.05).

sec.p: The Relative Median Potency (RMP) analysis was performed to statistically compare the LD50 values between experimental groups. As shown in Table 1, the 95% confidence intervals (CI) of LD50 estimates overlapped across all groups, suggesting no significant differences in acute toxicity. The RMP analysis (Table 2) confirmed this observation, as none of the comparisons showed statistical significance, with all 95% CI of RMP including the value 1. This indicates that neither compound or exposure route resulted in significantly different toxicity levels. These findings reinforce the conclusion that PTS and PTSO exhibit comparable acute toxicity profiles in short-lived spring honey bees, regardless of administration method.

caption.p: Relative Median Potency (RMP) analysis. RMP values represent the direct ratio of LD50 estimates between experimental groups. A RMP greater than 1 indicates that the first group has a higher LD50 (lower toxicity) than the second group. Statistical significance was assessed using 95% confidence intervals (CI). An interval including the value of 1 indicates no significant differences.

fn.p: No LD₅₀ were obtained for long-lived winter honey bees, as no mortality was observed at any of the tested concentrations.

sec.title: Voluntary intake of PTS and PTSO
sec.p: The results provide a test for antifeedant effects, which are important sublethal effects that might harm bee colonies. Figure 5 shows the amount of food ingested by each group of long-lived winter honey bees after 6 h, and the mortality observed after 24 h. After 48 h the mortality rate did not change. Each winter honey bee ate an average of 14.66 mg of sucrose solution (negative control) after 6 h, which represents 97.30% of the content of the feeder (200 µl). The average mortality of the negative control (sucrose solution) did not reach 10%. The mortality of the diluents acetone and polysorbate was less than 10%, which reaffirmed the suitability of using these compounds to dissolve both PTS and PTSO and dimethoate (toxic standard), respectively. Mortality of bees fed on dimethoate was 100%. The mortality of this cohort whose diet contained 10 µg a.i./µl showed significant differences compared with the negative control (p < 0.05). However, each individual ingested 0.29 and 1.11 mg of diet supplemented with PTS and PTSO, respectively (1.88% and 7.51%). This suggests that mortality was due to starvation. From the concentration of 4 µg a.i./µl, no significant differences were observed between the mortality of the groups that were fed with supplemented diet and the negative control. Although the intake of the groups fed on supplemented diet with 4 and 2 µg a.i./µl differed significantly from the intake of the negative control (p < 0.05), individuals of these 4 study groups ingested a minimum of 50% of the food. There were no significant differences between the negative control and the groups fed on supplemented diet with 1, 0.1, 0.05 and 0.01 µg a.i./µl, which ate more than 13 mg/bee (> 94% of the content of the feeder).

caption.p: Correlation of the voluntary intake of food, consisting of PTS and PTSO in sucrose solution at different concentrations, and mortality in long-lived winter honey bees, in comparison with the negative control (sucrose solution) and using dimethoate as toxicity standard. Intake and mortality results are expressed in mg/bee and as percentage, respectively. Values are means with SD in bars. Bars with asterisks indicate significant differences in intake compared to the negative control according to Dunnett’s test using a 95% confidence level (***p < 0.001; ****p < 0.0001). Bars with letters indicate significant differences in mortality rate compared to the negative control according to Dunnett’s test (p < 0.05).

sec.p: Voluntary intake and mortality data of short-lived spring honey bees are shown in Fig. 6. Each bee ate an average of 10.20 mg of sucrose solution after 24 h. Intake and mortality results from bees that were fed with polysorbate and acetone, as well as dimethoate and sucrose solution supplemented with 10 µg a.i./µl, followed the same pattern as the winter bee cohort. Furthermore, in this case a significant mortality was also observed in the groups in which the sucrose solution was supplemented with 4 µg a.i./µl (p < 0.05), in which individuals ate 5.20 mg PTS and 7.50 mg PTSO (47.33 and 66.18%). These intake percentages are similar to those of the winter bee cohort. However, in the case of long-lived winter honey bees, no significant differences were observed compared to the mortality of the negative control. This supports the results obtained in acute oral and contact toxicity tests, which indicate that the spring bee cohort is more sensitive to both active ingredients. At concentrations of 2 µg a.i./µl, no mortality was observed. In addition, no significant differences in intake were detected in bees fed diets supplemented with ≤1 µg a.i./µl compared to the negative control.

caption.p: Correlation of the voluntary intake of food, consisting of PTS and PTSO in sucrose solution at different concentrations, and mortality in short-lived spring honey bees, in comparison with the negative control (sucrose solution) and using dimethoate as toxicity standard. Intake and mortality results are expressed in mg/bee and as percentage, respectively. Values are means with SD in bars. Bars with asterisks indicate significant differences in intake compared to the negative control according to Dunnett’s test using a 95% confidence level (***p < 0.001; ****p < 0.0001). Bars with letters indicate significant differences in mortality rate compared to the negative control according to Dunnett’s test (p < 0.05).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Despite generally being considered safer, these agents have sometimes been found to negatively affect non-target organisms, such as pollinators, and arthropods and microorganisms used for biological control50. In a recent review, Giunti et al.51 emphasized the need to delve deeper into the detrimental effects of botanical control agents, which are typically rich in various active compounds. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report assessing the safety of PTS and PTSO from onion for the western honey bee, covering acute toxicity and antifeedant effect through voluntary intake, and comparing individuals’ response from two different seasons. As an exploratory study, our aim was not to generate regulatory endpoints such as NOAEL or GLP-compliant LD₅₀ datasets, but to characterize acute effects and feeding behaviour under field-relevant and OECD-defined testing conditions. In line with this objective, dose selection was driven by expected field exposure and mechanistic considerations rather than by regulatory requirements to generate benchmark endpoints. Within this exploratory scope, no deviations from the applicable OECD acute toxicity test guidelines were introduced.

In this study, we showed that PTS and PTSO do not cause mortality by contact or oral exposure at the proposed application dose (1000 µg/ml, i.e. 1 µg/bee) in either long-lived winter or short-lived spring honey bees. It should be noted that, despite 1000 µg/ml being the proposed application dose for field use, the tests carried out by our team on olive seedlings infected with V. dahliae already showed effects on all the parameters evaluated (incidence and severity of the disease, and population of the fungus in soil and vascular tissue) at concentrations of 250 and 500 µg/ml significant differences were observed compared with the control. However, the response of the spring bee cohort to the dose established by OECD guidelines to assess the acute oral and contact toxicity by limit test, 100 µg/bee (100,000 µg/ml), is different from that of the winter bee cohort. While none of the compounds resulted in a significant toxic effect when they were tested at 100 µg/bee in winter honey bees, contact or ingestion of one of them at that concentration caused 100% spring honey bee mortality after 24 h of exposure. This dose, set to evaluate product safety, represents a 100-fold increase over the hypothetical application dose under field conditions. In both LD50 determinations PTS was slightly more toxic than PTSO; however, this difference was not statistically significant. These results were not as expected, since in previous contact toxicity tests carried out on adult individuals of the cotton aphid, A. gossypii, PTSO showed greater biocidal activity than PTS34. Moreover, when comparing these results to common agrochemicals, PTS and PTSO exhibited higher LD50 values, indicating a lower toxicity. For instance, thiamethoxam has an LD50 of 0.005 µg/bee (oral) and a contact LD50 of 0.78 µg/bee. Similarly, abamectin has an LD50 of 0.0044 µg/bee (contact) and 0.0011 µg/bee (oral). Sulfoxaflor has an LD50 of 0.146 µg/bee (contact) and 2.65 µg/bee (oral)52. The lower toxicity values observed suggest that PTS and PTSO could be considered promising candidates for pest management strategies with a potentially reduced impact on pollinators.

The difference in susceptibility between long-lived winter and short-lived spring honey bees to PTS and PTSO may be related to their physiological differences. Winter honey bees have a considerably longer lifespan, since they emerge in late August, survive the winter, and initiate brood rearing in spring53. They have a larger fat body and therefore accumulate larger reserves of nutrients54, as well as a higher protein concentration in the haemolymph55. The protein content of winter and spring honey bees mainly differs in the concentration of vitellogenin, a storage protein that also has multiple regulatory roles in the body of the bee. It is synthesised in the fat body53. Vitellogenin is highly expressed during autumn and winter and is related to the greater longevity of winter honey bees56, it improves tolerance to starvation and protects cells from oxidative damage57,58. In addition, the fat body plays a key role in detoxification59. Cytochrome P450 enzymes are expressed in the fat body, as well as other tissues, and catalyse the oxidative detoxification of xenobiotics60. Consequently, the larger fat-body mass of winter bees likely provides greater P450-mediated detoxification capacity, which may underlie their lower susceptibility to PTS and PTSO.

In this study, the winter and spring cohorts differed in age. Adult winter honey bees, old bees that ensure the survival of the colony until spring, were collected from no-brood hive frames, since queens stop laying eggs after summer61. In contrast, in spring it was not possible to collect uniformly aged adult honey bees directly from the hive due to the high rate of egg laying. For spring honey bees, it was necessary to keep brood frames in incubators and collect emerged individuals, which were kept for 2 days in incubator until the start of the trials. Age is a critical factor when comparing susceptibility of winter and spring honey bee populations to PPPs59. It has been reported that cytochrome P450 activity increases progressively with worker age, showing that detoxification capacity is not fixed but varies with physiological condition, thereby altering susceptibility to insecticides across the worker lifespan62. Another factor that could increase the resistance of winter honey bees to PPPs compared to spring bees is the differential microbiota63. In recent years, several authors have suggested that gut microbiota contributes to insecticide resistance64,65, partly by inducing cytochrome P450 enzymes expression66. It has been demonstrated that the microbiota acquired in laboratory conditions is different from that acquired in the hive67. Furthermore, in honey bees the gut microbiota is established within the first 4–7 days post-emergence and becomes stable thereafter64,67. Therefore, the spring honey bees used in this study, emerged and reared in incubators, likely lacked a mature microbiota, unlike winter bees collected directly from the hive. The design of research comparing honey bees from different seasons is limited, as it was not possible to use adult bees of the same age for both populations. Lastly, the observed differences in susceptibility between the cohorts used in this study may also be influenced by their nutritional conditions at the onset of adulthood. While long-lived winter cohort had prior access to pollen and diverse nutrients before collection, whereas the short-lived spring cohort primarily relied on sugar solutions. Diet has been reported to modulate detoxification capacity in honey bees; in particular, pollen-derived flavonoids can influence xenobiotic metabolism68, which could contribute to the cohort-specific susceptibility observed. Specifically, pollen-derived flavonoids such as quercetin and kaempferol upregulate P450 expression and enhance metabolic processing of xenobiotics, leading to lower internal residues after exposure69,70.

Winter bees are naturally less exposed to agrochemicals, since their diet relies on stored honey and pollen, where pesticide residues occur at concentrations that minimise toxic risk71. Even so, comparing winter and spring bees under identical laboratory exposure remains valuable, since it highlights seasonal differences that are not attributable to environmental exposure.

Pesticide formulations often include more than one active ingredient. There is evidence that the simultaneous use of different active ingredients may have a toxic effect that is more than additive, i.e., could induce synergistic effects72. In this research, the risks associated with the joint use of PTS and PTSO in the formulation of PPPs have been assessed. Our data show that co-exposure to PTS and PTSO did not result in synergistic effects. While exposure to 50 µg PTS + 50 µg PTSO/bee did not cause an increase in toxicity compared to 100 µg/bee of one of the active ingredients, exposure to 100 µg PTS + 100 µg PTSO had an additive effect and doubled the mortality rate. This demonstrates the dose dependency of the mortality outcomes.

Feeder experiments play an important role in revealing the behaviour of honey bees to different substances. Understanding these responses is important to determine the potential risk that such substances pose to honey bees in agricultural systems73. In this study, we observed that both long-lived winter and short-lived spring honey bees do not voluntarily ingest feed supplemented with PTS or PTSO at 10,000 µg/ml. This suggests that both compounds exert a strong antifeedant effect at high concentrations, preventing honey bees from ingesting them voluntarily or accidentally. This is an advantage, since at that concentration both PTS and PTSO caused around 50% mortality. The intake of both honey bee cohorts, whose diet was supplemented with 1000 µg/ml or less, was nearly 100% and did not significantly differ from the intake of the negative control group, fed with unsupplemented diet. At these concentrations, no mortality or sublethal damage were observed. These data corroborate the results obtained in the acute oral toxicity evaluation using limit test and suggest that, at the proposed application dose for field use, neither PTS nor PTSO alter the feeding or foraging and recruitment activity of honey bees. The effect of both compounds was quite homogeneous in terms of repellent activity, since no significant differences were observed between the intake of PTS and PTSO by individuals from the same season. In agreement with these results, in a previous study we observed that at 0.5 µg/µl PTS and PTSO exerted a similar repellent effect on the cotton aphid, A. gossypii34. Furthermore, it has been reported that onion and garlic volatile compounds alter field behaviour of A. gossypii but do not affect its main predator, ladybirds, from the family of beetles Coccinellidae74. The repellent properties of onion-derived compounds, as well as from other species of the genus Allium, such as garlic (Allium sativum) or leek (Allium porrum), have been widely described against other pests including the green aphid Myzus persicae Sulzer (Hemiptera: Aphididae), the wheat aphid Sitobion avenae Fabricius (Hemiptera: Aphididae), the mealworm beetle Tenebrio molitor Linnaeus (Coleoptera: Tenebrionidae) and the black fungus gnat Lycoriella ingénue Dufour (Diptera: Sciaridae)75,76. Nevertheless, there is a scarcity of studies reporting this repellent effect in pollinators. In our research, we provide specific insights into two active compounds from Allium, underscoring the need for further research on their long-term impacts.

Previous studies have suggested that plant derived compounds may be effective in controlling pathogens/parasites threatening honey bees77. Growth inhibition of bee pathogens Paenibacillus larvae and Ascosphaera apis by allicin derived from garlic has been assessed in vitro78. These assays did not report the effect of the compound on honey bees. In our research, we establish the doses at which PTS and PTSO derived from onion did not result in toxic effects or alteration of the feeding of long-lived winter and short-lived spring honey bees. Taking this into account, in future trials the effect of PTS and PTSO on bee pathogens and parasites could be evaluated at safe concentrations according to what was established in this study.

Finally, numerous studies have confirmed PTS and PTSO as effective flavor enhancers for food and feed, leading to comprehensive toxicological safety assessments. These evaluations consistently show that neither compound poses significant toxic risks in cellular or animal models, including no evidence of oral, subchronic or mutagenic toxicity37,38,40,79. This extensive research supports the safe inclusion of PTS and PTSO in the agri-food industry for human and animal consumption, including honey bees, enhancing their status as botanical additives. However, their application may be limited by their strong taste and odor, which should be considered in practical uses.

A previous study conducted by our team demonstrated, through HPLC–UV quantification, the low persistence of both PTS and PTSO in soil, as these compounds volatilize rapidly after application34. This suggests that their potential for accumulation in plant matrices such as nectar and pollen, which could affect honey bees, may also be limited. Nevertheless, future studies should specifically evaluate whether PTS and PTSO residues can be transferred to these matrices to fully understand their impact on honey bee colonies and other pollinators37,80.

In conclusion, this study provides the first in vivo evaluation of the acute toxicity and antifeedant activity of the onion-derived organosulfur compounds PTS and PTSO in the western honey bee. Both compounds showed low acute toxicity and no change in feeding behaviour at field-relevant concentrations. A clear difference in susceptibility between seasonal cohorts was observed, with winter honey bees being more tolerant than spring bees, which to our knowledge has not been previously reported for any substance and highlights the importance of physiological and environmental factors when evaluating plant protection products. Adverse effects were limited to non-field-relevant concentrations. Furthermore, no synergism between PTS and PTSO was detected at any concentration tested. These findings suggest that both compounds could be compatible with honey-bee safety under acute exposure and support their potential for environmentally friendly pest-management applications. Within the EFSA (2023) tiered risk-assessment framework, this type of acute, laboratory-based study represents only an initial line of evidence and, on its own, is not sufficient to support formal regulatory acceptance. A full regulatory risk assessment would additionally require GLP-compliant chronic, colony-level and multi-species studies conducted under the full EFSA (2023) guidance and relevant OECD test guidelines, together with the generation of benchmark regulatory endpoints (e.g. NOAEL), which were beyond the scope of the present exploratory study. Further research is necessary, including colony-level and chronic exposure studies, as the application doses do not prevent ingestion, exposure-based risk-quotient estimation, comparisons with antimicrobial agents currently used in agriculture and evaluation of potential effects on beneficial bee-associated microbiota. In line with EFSA guidance, studies on other pollinators, such as bumblebees and solitary bees, are also necessary, since this research is specific to A. mellifera.

sec.title: Compounds and reagents
sec.p: PTS (CAS: 1948-52-3) and PTSO (CAS: 1113–13-9) from A. cepa at 20% purity, supported in polysorbate 80, were provided by DOMCA S.A.U. Polysorbate 80 (CAS: 9005–65-6), acetone ≥ 97% (CAS: 67–64-1) and dimethoate (CAS: 60–51-5) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich Química S.L. (Madrid, Spain).

sec.title: Honey bees
sec.p: The experiments presented here were carried out in February and June 2023. Adult honey bees were used in all experiments. They were obtained from an experimental apiary of the Centro de Investigación Apícola y Agroambiental (CIAPA) in Marchamalo (Castilla-La Mancha, Spain). Considering the annual life cycle of the honey bee colony, the method by which the adult honey bees were picked depended on the season. Since egg laying slows down considerably during winter, winter honey bees, emerged in the fall, were picked at 9 a.m. during the month of February from no-brood frames by brushing them into cardboard boxes and taken immediately to the laboratory according to Martín-Hernández et al. (2007), where they were caged (see below)81. Spring honey bees were collected during the month of June from frames of capped brood, whicht were kept in an incubator at 35 ± 1 °C82. After 24 h, emergent adult honey bees were removed from the brood combs and placed in cylindrical steel mesh cages (175 mm long, 45 mm in diameter)83, that were kept in an incubator for 2 days at 25 ± 1 °C and at a relative humidity of 85 ± 5%81. During this time, bees were fed ad libitum with 50% (w/v) sucrose solution in water83. This method ensured that spring bees had a uniform age of 2 days at the start of the experiment. Winter bees were also uniform in age due to the absence of brood rearing during winter having survived since the fall, but they were older and had a longer lifespan compared to spring bees, which represent a younger cohort.

The cages had a 9.5 mm diameter hole in one of the bases that allowed the introduction of a conical tube containing the food83. In order to facilitate honey bee handling, to perform the different experiments, long-lived winter and short-lived spring honey bees were anaesthetised with carbon dioxide. They were randomly distributed into groups of 15 and confined to steel mesh cages as previously described. Only healthy bees not exerting any clinical sign of disease were used for toxicity tests. They were conducted according to OECD Test Guidelines 213 and 214, which are the validated and internationally accepted protocols referenced by EFSA for acute toxicity assessments in A. mellifera.

sec.title: Acute contact toxicity test
sec.p: Acute contact toxicity of PTS and PTSO was assessed by a limit test according to OECD Guideline for the Testing of Chemicals in Honeybees84. The limit test was performed using dilutions of each active ingredient (a.i.) at 100 µg/µl (as established by the guideline) and 1 µg/µl (hypothetical application dose for field use) in water, so that both the OECD-recommended screening dose and the expected field exposure level were covered. Additionally, the synergy between PTS and PTSO was evaluated. Blend solutions were prepared with PTS and PTSO at 50 µg/µl and 0.5 µg/µl each, so that two solutions with a final concentration of 100 µg a.i./µl and 1 µg a.i./µl were obtained. The toxicity of two blends of PTS and PTSO at 100 and 1 µg a.i./µl each was also studied. Dimethoate at 0.3 µg/µl in acetone was used as toxic standard. The toxicity of acetone and polysorbate, which were used as diluents for dimethoate and PTS and PTSO, respectively, was also evaluated to verify that these did not have a negative effect on honey bees by themselves. Double-distilled water was used as control. Dilutions used in the limit test are shown in Table 3. For each test dose and control, three replicates cages containing 15 bees each were included. A volume of 1 µl of the corresponding dilution was applied to the thorax of anaesthetised bees using a micropipette. After application, bees were placed in the corresponding cage and held in an incubator (Memmert® Mod. IPP500, Schwabach, Germany) in the dark at 25 ± 1 °C. They were fed with sucrose solution ad libitum during the test period. Mortality was recorded after 24 h and 48 h. In cases where mortality was observed, a full study was carried out to calculate the median lethal dose (LD50).

sec.p: For the determination of LD50, bees were exposed to a range of doses of the test substances dissolved in water. To ensure that the LD50 range was covered, a range-finding test was conducted with PTS and PTSO at the following concentrations: 100; 90; 80; 70; 60; 50; 40; 30; 20; 10; and 1 µg/µl. This range-finding test enabled the choice of the appropriate doses for the determination of LD50: 80; 53.3; 35.5; 23.7; 15.8; and 10.5 µg/µl. Bees were treated by topical application and mortality was recorded following the same procedure. The same controls and number of replicates were included.
Live honey bees were observed for sublethal damage. Specifically, difficulty in flying, atypical muscle movements, and drowsiness were assessed.
Tests were considered invalid if the average mortality for the total number of bees in the different control groups exceeded 10% as recommended in the OECD 1998 guideline.

sec.title: Acute oral toxicity test
sec.p: Acute oral toxicity of PTS and PTSO was assessed by a limit test according to OECD Guideline for the Testing of Chemicals in Honeybees85, with some modifications. Just as for the determination of acute contact toxicity, a limit test was carried out in which the same concentrations of active ingredients, previously described in Table 3, were evaluated. In this case, dilutions were prepared in sucrose solution. The same toxic standard was used, and acetone and polysorbate, used as solvents for dimethoate and PTS and PTSO, were also included in the test. Sucrose solution was used as control. Three cages containing 15 bees each were used per test dose/control. Bees were deprived of food for 2 h before treatment so that their intestinal contents at the beginning of the test were similar. They were disoriented by applying carbon dioxide so that they were not anesthetised. Next, a volume of 1 µl of the corresponding dilution was provided to each bee directly in the mouth using a micropipette. It was verified that the bees appropriately ingested the provided volume. After administration of the test doses, bees were given sucrose solution ad libitum as food throughout the test period. Mortality was recorded after 24 h and 48 h. In cases where mortality was observed, a full study was carried out to calculate the LD50.

LD50 was assessed by oral exposure of bees to a wide range of doses of PTS and PTSO dissolved in sucrose solution: 100; 80; 60; 40; 20; 10; and 1 µg/µl. This range-finding test allowed us to establish appropriate concentrations for the assay. In a second trial, the mortality of bees exposed to PTS and PTSO at 30; 25; 20; 15; 10; 5; and 1 µg/µl was determined. The same procedure, replicates and controls were used.
Live honey bees were observed for sublethal damage. Difficulty in flying, atypical muscle movements, and drowsiness were assessed.
Tests were considered invalid if the average mortality for the total number of bees in the different control groups exceeded 10%.

sec.title: Determination of voluntary intake
sec.p: To determine if the honey bees feed willingly on the products tested, the voluntarily fed of different concentrations of PTS and PTSO by bees was studied according to OECD Guideline for the Testing of Chemicals in Honeybees85. To that end, 2 h starved bees were exposed to the following concentrations of each compound prepared in sucrose solution: 10; 4; 2; 1; 0.1; 0.05; and 0.01 µg/µl. Dimethoate at 0.3 µg/µl in acetone was used as toxic standard, and sucrose solution, acetone and polysorbate were used as controls. Each group was made up of three cages with 15 bees each. The weight of the feeders was recorded before and after depositing 200 µl of the corresponding dilution. The feeders were then attached to the bases of the cages. After 6 h in the case of long-lived winter bees and 24 h in the case of short-lived spring bees, the feeders were removed from the cages and weighed in order to assess the amount of treated diet consumed (mg food/bee). Afterwards, the tested products were removed and fresh sucrose solution was provided ad libitum and mortality was recorded 24 h and 48 h after the feeders containing the treatments were removed.

The exposure time to the treated diet was adapted to the needs of each cohort. In a preliminary test, it was found that the winter bee cohort, collected directly from the hive, quickly ingested the sucrose solution. However, the short-lived spring bee cohort, which emerged from frames kept in incubators, needed 24 h to ingest the same amount of food.

sec.title: Statistical treatment
sec.p: GraphPad prism 8.0 software (GraphPad Software Inc., San Diego, California) was used for conducting the ANOVA tests. IBM SPSS Statistics V21.0 (IBM Corporation, Armonk, New York) was used for calculating and comparing the LD50 values. A one-way ANOVA test supplemented with Tukey’s post hoc was used for the evaluation of statistically significant differences between mortality percentages observed in Limits Tests. The LD50 values were calculated using probit regression with a confidence level of 95%. The Relative Median Potency (RMP) method was used to establish significant differences between the LD50 data, with a 95% confidence interval for all comparisons. A one-way ANOVA test supplemented with Dunnett’s post hoc was used to compare the amount of treated diet voluntarily ingested, as well as the recorded mortality, with the data of the control group. Differences were considered statistically significant when p < 0.05.
